lessons.title: Reading Gaussian contours
lessons.deck: Review the geometry; the equal-variance/circle teach-back is still pending.

prerequisites.title: Covariance matrix
prerequisites.detail: Diagonal entries are variances; off-diagonal entries are covariances.

prerequisites.title: Density
prerequisites.detail: A contour joins equal densities, not equal point probabilities.

lessons.teachback: Why do equal variances not guarantee circular Gaussian contours?

lessons.title: The Gamma function and Gamma distribution
lessons.deck: A positive-valued density, with a short factorial bridge and careful rate/scale notation.

prerequisites.title: Factorials
prerequisites.detail: n! multiplies integers from 1 through n; 0! = 1.

prerequisites.title: Integration
prerequisites.detail: A continuous density has total area 1; probabilities are interval areas.

prerequisites.title: Exponentials
prerequisites.detail: exp(z) means e raised to z; negative exponents give decay.

lessons.teachback: Explain the difference between the Gamma function and a Gamma distribution. If the rate doubles at fixed shape, what happens to the mean?

lessons.title: From Bernoulli to categorical
lessons.deck: Several possible categories, one realised outcome.

prerequisites.title: Bernoulli
prerequisites.detail: A binary outcome is 0 or 1; theta is its success probability.

prerequisites.title: Normalisation
prerequisites.detail: Probabilities of mutually exclusive, exhaustive outcomes sum to 1.

lessons.teachback: For three categories with probabilities 0.2, 0.3 and 0.5, what is observed on one trial, and what are the parameters?

lessons.title: The Beta distribution
lessons.deck: A continuous distribution over a probability parameter—not a binary outcome.

prerequisites.title: Density versus mass
prerequisites.detail: Density height is not a point probability.

prerequisites.title: Gamma function
prerequisites.detail: Gamma factors provide a normalising constant.

prerequisites.title: Parameter versus observation
prerequisites.detail: A Bernoulli observation is binary; its parameter may be anywhere from 0 to 1.

lessons.teachback: How can theta have a continuous Beta distribution while a Bernoulli observation remains only 0 or 1?

lessons.title: Probability rules behind Bayesian learning
lessons.deck: Identify the unknowns, then distinguish joint, conditional and marginal distributions.

prerequisites.title: Random variable versus observation
prerequisites.detail: A variable describes possible values; an observation is the value actually recorded.

prerequisites.title: Density versus probability
prerequisites.detail: For continuous variables, interval areas are probabilities; density at a point is not a point probability.

lessons.teachback: Explain joint, conditional and marginal distributions, then derive Bayes’ rule from the product rule.

lessons.title: Maximum likelihood and plug-in prediction
lessons.deck: A single best-fitting parameter is useful, but it is not a description of parameter uncertainty.

prerequisites.title: Likelihood
prerequisites.detail: Keep the recorded data fixed and vary candidate parameter values.

prerequisites.title: Logarithms and argmax
prerequisites.detail: Log preserves the location of a positive likelihood’s maximum; argmax returns the parameter, not its likelihood value.

lessons.teachback: Why can 3 heads out of 5 and 300 heads out of 500 have the same MLE but very different parameter uncertainty?

lessons.title: Specify, update, integrate and predict
lessons.deck: Unpack slide 6 and derive the evidence calculation from probability rules.

prerequisites.title: Marginalisation
prerequisites.detail: Integrate an unwanted continuous variable out of a joint density.

prerequisites.title: Prior and likelihood
prerequisites.detail: The prior describes parameters before these data; the likelihood describes data given parameters.

lessons.teachback: Why is the evidence a prior-weighted average, while prediction after observing data is a posterior-weighted average?

lessons.title: Learning a Gaussian mean: likelihood and MLE
lessons.deck: Keep observation variance known while estimating the shared mean.

prerequisites.title: Gaussian parameters
prerequisites.detail: The mean sets the centre; the variance describes spread of observations around that centre.

prerequisites.title: Differentiation
prerequisites.detail: An interior maximum has zero derivative; the second derivative checks curvature.

lessons.teachback: Derive the Gaussian mean MLE and distinguish known observation variance from uncertainty about the unknown mean.

lessons.title: Choosing a prior and understanding conjugacy
lessons.deck: Separate scientific beliefs, structural preferences and computational convenience.

prerequisites.title: Support
prerequisites.detail: A distribution’s support describes which values are allowed by the model.

prerequisites.title: Gaussian density
prerequisites.detail: A Gaussian is a distribution over a real-valued variable; that variable can itself be an unknown parameter.

lessons.teachback: What are hyperparameters, and why does conjugacy depend on both the likelihood and the parameter being inferred?

lessons.title: Deriving the Gaussian posterior by completing the square
lessons.deck: Likelihood information and prior information combine through additive precisions.

prerequisites.title: Completing the square
prerequisites.detail: A quadratic Aμ²−2Bμ can be written A(μ−B/A)²−B²/A.

prerequisites.title: Precision
prerequisites.detail: Precision is inverse variance: greater precision means less uncertainty.

lessons.teachback: Derive the Gaussian posterior’s additive precision and explain why its mean is a precision-weighted compromise.

lessons.title: Reading the Gaussian mean update plot
lessons.deck: Explain the centre, width and height of every curve on slide 12.

prerequisites.title: Posterior mean and variance
prerequisites.detail: The mean is the centre of parameter uncertainty; the variance quantifies its spread.

prerequisites.title: Density normalisation
prerequisites.detail: A narrowing density becomes taller while retaining total area one.

lessons.teachback: Why does the plotted posterior become narrow near 2 while the observations can still vary substantially?

lessons.title: Predicting a future Gaussian observation
lessons.deck: The predictive variance contains observation noise plus uncertainty about the mean.

prerequisites.title: Posterior integration
prerequisites.detail: Average conditional predictions over the posterior rather than choosing only one parameter.

prerequisites.title: Variance of independent sums
prerequisites.detail: Independent variances add; this differs from adding precisions when estimating a common mean.

lessons.teachback: Why is the Gaussian predictive variance σ² + σ_N², and why does it not approach zero as the dataset grows?

lessons.title: Bernoulli likelihood, counts and boundary estimates
lessons.deck: Learn a success probability from a sequence of binary observations.

prerequisites.title: Binary outcomes
prerequisites.detail: Each observation is 0 or 1; its success probability θ can take any value between 0 and 1.

prerequisites.title: Products and powers
prerequisites.detail: Repeated success factors multiply to θ raised to the number of successes.

lessons.teachback: Derive the Bernoulli MLE, explain the all-heads boundary case, and distinguish a sequence likelihood from a binomial count probability.

lessons.title: Beta priors: location, concentration and shapes
lessons.deck: Separate an initial preferred success probability from the strength of that preference.

prerequisites.title: Gamma function
prerequisites.detail: Gamma factors normalise the Beta density; Γ(n)=(n−1)! for positive integers.

prerequisites.title: Density on an interval
prerequisites.detail: The Beta variable is a continuous probability parameter, not a binary outcome.

lessons.teachback: Why do Beta(8,2) and Beta(80,20) have the same mean but different uncertainty, and what does “pseudo-count” mean?

lessons.title: Deriving the Beta–Bernoulli posterior
lessons.deck: Add observed counts, interpret weighted means, and distinguish posterior summaries.

prerequisites.title: Beta density
prerequisites.detail: Its kernel is θ^(α−1)(1−θ)^(β−1).

prerequisites.title: Proportionality
prerequisites.detail: A kernel omits constants independent of θ; the normalised density must still integrate to one.

lessons.teachback: Derive the count update and explain why the posterior mean, MLE and MAP can be different.

lessons.title: Four priors, one dataset: reading every update
lessons.deck: Compare weak, symmetric, biased and strongly misleading priors on slides 19–22.

prerequisites.title: Conjugate updating
prerequisites.detail: Add successes to α and failures to β.

prerequisites.title: Prior strength
prerequisites.detail: The sum α+β determines the relative prior weight in the posterior mean.

lessons.teachback: Using the four plotted priors, explain why the same data can yield different posterior beliefs and why a confident prior need not be accurate.

lessons.title: Recognising the bandit lab without doing it
lessons.deck: Connect priors, posteriors and sampling to the upcoming exercise; stop before lab work.

prerequisites.title: Inference versus sampling
prerequisites.detail: A posterior is a distribution; sampling draws possible values from that distribution.

prerequisites.title: Bernoulli and Gamma observations
prerequisites.detail: Bernoulli models binary values; Gamma can model positive continuous observations.

lessons.teachback: Explain the difference between sampling a parameter from a posterior and sampling an observation from a model.

lessons.title: Separate inference from decisions
lessons.deck: Probabilistic outputs make the boundary between evidence and action visible.

prerequisites.title: Classification and regression
prerequisites.detail: Classification predicts categories; regression predicts numerical quantities.

prerequisites.title: Predictive uncertainty
prerequisites.detail: A predictive distribution represents possible future observations, not a guaranteed outcome.

lessons.teachback: Why might two people agree on a 70% probability but reasonably choose different actions?

lessons.title: A good decision can have a bad outcome
lessons.deck: Judge reasoning using the information available before the result; retain class probabilities for later decisions.

prerequisites.title: Probability-weighted averages
prerequisites.detail: Expected loss averages consequences across possible outcomes.

prerequisites.title: Inference versus decision
prerequisites.detail: A probability estimate describes uncertainty; an action also requires consequences and context.

lessons.teachback: An action chosen to minimise expected loss produces a bad result. What would you inspect before calling the original decision foolish?

lessons.title: When the population changes, the probability changes
lessons.deck: Recalibrate the lecture’s 95% trial prediction to about 2%, with the required assumptions.

prerequisites.title: Bayes’ rule
prerequisites.detail: Posterior class probabilities combine within-class likelihoods with class prevalence.

prerequisites.title: Odds
prerequisites.detail: Odds p/(1−p) compare a probability with its complement; probability is odds/(1+odds).

prerequisites.title: Population shift
prerequisites.detail: The simple correction assumes only class prevalence changes, not the within-class feature distributions.

lessons.teachback: How can the same features give 95% in a balanced trial but about 2% in the general population? State the required assumption.

lessons.title: Choose actions using expected costs
lessons.deck: Derive the medical and fraud thresholds from the lecture’s cost matrices.

prerequisites.title: Expectation
prerequisites.detail: Average an action’s losses using the probabilities of the true states.

prerequisites.title: Cost matrices
prerequisites.detail: Rows give true states and columns give proposed actions; entries are losses, not probabilities.

prerequisites.title: Simple inequalities
prerequisites.detail: Compare the two expected losses and solve for the probability threshold.

lessons.teachback: Derive the 4% medical threshold and explain why it does not mean a patient above that threshold is probably diseased.

lessons.title: False independence: the Sally Clark case study
lessons.deck: Inspect the assumption behind multiplying rare-event probabilities and distinguish evidence from hypothesis probability.

prerequisites.title: Product rule
prerequisites.detail: P(A,B)=P(A)P(B|A); replacing the conditional by a marginal requires independence.

prerequisites.title: Shared latent variables
prerequisites.detail: Two events can be dependent overall even if independent given a shared unknown cause.

prerequisites.title: Likelihood versus posterior
prerequisites.detail: P(evidence|hypothesis) is not generally P(hypothesis|evidence).

lessons.teachback: Which assumption allows the one-in-8,543 probability to be squared, and how could a shared unknown condition invalidate it?

lessons.title: A fictional experiment makes clustering visible
lessons.deck: Reproduce the slide’s arithmetic, identify its denominator ambiguity, and define a clean dependent-event example.

prerequisites.title: Events and denominators
prerequisites.detail: Define whether a number counts occurrences per example or the probability of a specified binary event.

prerequisites.title: Conditional probability
prerequisites.detail: Knowing A can change the probability of B; this is incompatible with independence.

lessons.teachback: In the labelled A/B dataset, why is the pair probability 0.001 rather than 0.001²? What makes the slide’s 250-fold arithmetic convention-dependent?

lessons.title: Selection effects and p-values: the Lucia de Berk case study
lessons.deck: Read the two tables critically and distinguish null tail probabilities from posterior beliefs.

prerequisites.title: Null model and tail events
prerequisites.detail: A p-value measures a test statistic at least as extreme under a specified null procedure.

prerequisites.title: Selection mechanisms
prerequisites.detail: A subject chosen in advance differs from the most unusual subject found after searching.

prerequisites.title: Expected counts
prerequisites.detail: Across m comparable null tests, a tail probability q gives expected count mq.

lessons.teachback: Why does a rare pattern for a nurse chosen in advance differ from a rare-looking pattern found after a large search, and why is neither a posterior guilt probability?

lessons.title: Correlation is not an instruction for intervention
lessons.deck: Interpret the student scatter plot and the proposed common-cause graph without claiming a causal effect from association.

prerequisites.title: Correlation
prerequisites.detail: An association describes patterns among observations, not automatically an effect of changing a variable.

prerequisites.title: Graphical models
prerequisites.detail: A common cause can influence two observed variables.

prerequisites.title: Observation versus intervention
prerequisites.detail: Selecting people with an observed value differs from changing that value in comparable people.

lessons.teachback: Why does observing that slower students score lower not establish that forcing a student to finish sooner would improve their mark?

lessons.title: Simpson’s paradox: different mixtures, different totals
lessons.deck: Use the admissions counts and weighted averages, with an explicit correction to the source’s Medicine claim.

prerequisites.title: Conditional rates
prerequisites.detail: Acceptance within a department and acceptance across all departments use different denominators.

prerequisites.title: Weighted averages
prerequisites.detail: The aggregate rate weights each department’s rate by its share of applications.

prerequisites.title: Confounding
prerequisites.detail: A third variable can complicate an apparent relationship between the variables of interest.

lessons.teachback: Explain how different subgroup weights can reverse an aggregate comparison. What discrepancy should you mention in the lecture’s Medicine row?

lessons.title: Age confounding and the lecture’s closing message
lessons.deck: Read the dated vaccination graph as a confounding lesson, then consolidate Lecture 4 and preview regression.

prerequisites.title: Simpson’s paradox
prerequisites.detail: Aggregate rates can reverse within-group patterns when mixture weights differ.

prerequisites.title: Causal interpretation
prerequisites.detail: A graph’s causal assumptions do not by themselves provide an effect size or current medical guidance.

lessons.teachback: How can age reverse an aggregate comparison without contradicting within-age-group rates? Then name the separate inference and decision stages.

lessons.title: Regression and linear-in-parameter models
lessons.deck: Predict a real-valued target using a weighted sum of fixed functions.

prerequisites.title: Functions and observations
prerequisites.detail: A function maps an input x to an output. An observed target can differ from its underlying noise-free value.

prerequisites.title: Weighted sums
prerequisites.detail: Multiply each component by its weight and add the results; weights are adjustable parameters.

lessons.teachback: What makes a regression model linear in its parameters, even when its curve is not a straight line?

lessons.title: Choosing and reading basis functions
lessons.deck: Fixed input transformations supply the building blocks of the fitted curve.

prerequisites.title: Powers and polynomials
prerequisites.detail: x squared and higher powers transform an input nonlinearly while their coefficients can still enter linearly.

prerequisites.title: Exponentials
prerequisites.detail: exp(0)=1; increasingly negative exponents give values approaching zero.

lessons.teachback: Explain the roles of an RBF centre, its width and its weight. Which are fixed and which are learned in this lecture?

lessons.title: Least squares: from residuals to the normal equations
lessons.deck: Build the design matrix, check dimensions and derive the fitted weights.

prerequisites.title: Vectors, transpose and matrix multiplication
prerequisites.detail: Treat weights and targets as column vectors. Transpose swaps matrix rows and columns; inner dimensions must match.

prerequisites.title: Squared norm
prerequisites.detail: The squared Euclidean norm of a vector is the sum of its squared entries.

prerequisites.title: Gradient and rank
prerequisites.detail: A gradient lists partial derivatives. Full column rank means no design-matrix column is redundant.

lessons.teachback: Derive the least-squares normal equations and explain exactly when the displayed inverse formula is valid.

lessons.title: Interpolation is not the same as generalisation
lessons.deck: Understand why an exact fit can be a poor explanation of noisy observations.

prerequisites.title: Training error
prerequisites.detail: Training error measures fit to the observations used to choose the weights.

prerequisites.title: Noise and underlying signal
prerequisites.detail: A noisy observation need not equal the function value we want to recover.

lessons.teachback: Why does zero training error not establish that a fitted function will predict new targets well?

lessons.title: Ridge regularisation and the role of lambda
lessons.deck: Trade squared fitting error against squared weight size.

prerequisites.title: Quadratic objectives and gradients
prerequisites.detail: The derivative of one half times a squared weight is that weight.

prerequisites.title: Identity and positive definiteness
prerequisites.detail: I leaves a vector unchanged. A positive-definite matrix has positive quadratic form in every nonzero direction.

lessons.teachback: Derive the ridge solution, explain both extremes of lambda, and say why smaller weights are a modelling preference rather than a universal smoothness theorem.

lessons.title: Selecting lambda using held-out observations
lessons.deck: Distinguish fitting, hyperparameter selection and final evaluation.

prerequisites.title: Held-out evaluation
prerequisites.detail: Data not used to fit the weights can provide evidence about predictions beyond the training sample.

prerequisites.title: Root mean square error
prerequisites.detail: RMS error is the square root of the average squared residual; lower is better for that metric.

lessons.teachback: Explain why we use validation rather than training error to select lambda, and why the test set must not become another tuning set.

lessons.title: Gaussian noise turns least squares into maximum likelihood
lessons.deck: Build the regression likelihood and derive its squared-error objective.

prerequisites.title: Gaussian mean and variance
prerequisites.detail: Adding zero-mean Gaussian noise shifts a deterministic prediction into a Gaussian distribution over targets.

prerequisites.title: Conditional independence and logarithms
prerequisites.detail: Independent noise terms permit a product likelihood; log turns products into sums without changing maximisers.

lessons.teachback: Derive the negative log-likelihood and explain why its weight estimate equals least squares. Are targets at different fixed inputs identically distributed?

lessons.title: A Gaussian prior over the weights
lessons.deck: Replace an informal preference for small weights with an explicit distribution.

prerequisites.title: Precision versus variance
prerequisites.detail: Precision is inverse variance. A larger precision gives a narrower Gaussian.

prerequisites.title: Multivariate Gaussian
prerequisites.detail: A covariance matrix describes the spread and relationships across components of a vector.

lessons.teachback: What does alpha control, why is it a hyperparameter, and how can an independent weight prior produce correlated fitted function values?

lessons.title: Deriving the Gaussian posterior over weights
lessons.deck: Complete the matrix square to obtain both mean and covariance.

prerequisites.title: Bayes and conjugacy
prerequisites.detail: Posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior. Gaussian conjugacy means the resulting weight posterior is also Gaussian.

prerequisites.title: Completing the square
prerequisites.detail: A quadratic and a linear term can be rewritten as a quadratic centred on a suitable mean.

prerequisites.title: Matrix dimensions and positive definiteness
prerequisites.detail: The posterior precision is an M by M symmetric positive-definite matrix when alpha and noise variance are positive.

lessons.teachback: Derive the posterior precision, mean and covariance. Which quantity does the covariance describe, and why can its off-diagonal terms be nonzero?

lessons.title: MAP estimation and its exact connection to ridge
lessons.deck: Understand the useful shortcut—and the uncertainty it discards.

prerequisites.title: Mode and mean
prerequisites.detail: The mode maximises density. It equals the mean for this nondegenerate Gaussian, but not for every distribution.

prerequisites.title: Logarithms and constants
prerequisites.detail: A normalising factor independent of weights does not change the maximising weight vector.

lessons.teachback: Derive lambda = sigma-squared times alpha under this lecture’s objective convention. Why is retaining only MAP not the full Bayesian result?

lessons.title: Sequential learning in weight space and function space
lessons.deck: Read every stage of the lecture’s prior-to-posterior demonstration.

prerequisites.title: Conditional independence
prerequisites.detail: New observation likelihoods multiply when noise terms are independent given the same weights and model.

prerequisites.title: Gaussian contours
prerequisites.detail: Contours join equal density. Smaller contours at comparable density levels indicate more concentrated parameter uncertainty.

prerequisites.title: Function samples
prerequisites.detail: Sample a whole weight vector, then use the fixed basis functions to produce a whole curve.

lessons.teachback: Explain why sequential and batch updating agree, then narrate what changes in each column from the prior to 7, 8, 15 and 200 observations.

lessons.title: What Lecture 5 establishes—and what remains a preview
lessons.deck: Separate the completed posterior derivation from the later prediction and model-selection agenda.

prerequisites.title: Point estimate versus distribution
prerequisites.detail: The mean or mode is one vector; a posterior also describes uncertainty and relationships around it.

prerequisites.title: Hyperparameters and model choices
prerequisites.detail: Alpha, noise variance and fixed RBF width play different roles from the fitted weights.

lessons.teachback: Explain what full Bayesian regression adds beyond the ridge weight vector, and name the three topics that this lecture signposts rather than derives.

lessons.title: Why a MAP curve is not the whole Bayesian answer
lessons.deck: See why an identical fitted mean can hide missing parameter uncertainty.

prerequisites.title: Before this lesson
prerequisites.detail: Lecture 5 gave a Gaussian posterior over regression weights. Its mean and mode coincide, and equal a penalised least-squares estimate. Recall that a probability distribution contains more information than its maximum.

lessons.teachback: Explain why the same fitted curve can arise from PLS and MAP without making the two frameworks identical. What uncertainty is lost when only that curve is kept?

lessons.title: Rebuild the Gaussian linear-regression model
lessons.deck: Recover the weight posterior and its regularisation interpretation.

prerequisites.title: Before this lesson
prerequisites.detail: Recall a design matrix: row n is the feature vector at input x_n. Distinguish covariance from precision and observation noise from weight uncertainty.

lessons.teachback: Define the shapes of Phi, mu, Sigma and the two identity matrices in the model. Why is alpha a precision, and what is lambda?

lessons.title: The full predictive distribution and its nuisance variables
lessons.deck: Average weights, prior precision and noise to predict a new observation.

prerequisites.title: Before this lesson
prerequisites.detail: Use the sum/product rules and Bayes’ rule. A nuisance variable is an unknown that is not the final quantity being predicted, not an irrelevant quantity.

lessons.teachback: Write the fully Bayesian predictive integral and explain the roles of likelihood, weight prior, hyperpriors and the normalising evidence.

lessons.title: A ladder of predictions and the analytic roadblock
lessons.deck: Audit which unknowns each prediction framework retains.

prerequisites.title: Before this lesson
prerequisites.detail: Keep a distinction between fitting a parameter, retaining a parameter posterior, and using that posterior in a predictive integral.

lessons.teachback: Compare orthodox, MAP, fixed-hyperparameter Bayesian, Type-II and full Bayesian prediction. Which uncertainty does each keep or discard?

lessons.title: Type-II inference: exact factorisation, point approximation
lessons.deck: Separate exact factorisation from a hyperparameter point approximation.

prerequisites.title: Before this lesson
prerequisites.detail: Recall conditional probability factorisation and a Dirac delta: integrating a function against a point mass evaluates the function at that point.

lessons.teachback: Identify the exact and approximate steps in Type-II inference. Explain why flat log-priors require a parameterisation caveat when discussing a posterior mode.

lessons.title: Derive the Gaussian marginal likelihood
lessons.deck: Integrate weights to obtain the dataset covariance and density.

prerequisites.title: Before this lesson
prerequisites.detail: Recall that independent Gaussian random vectors add their covariances, and that multiplying a Gaussian vector by a matrix transforms its covariance.

lessons.teachback: Derive C = sigma² I + alpha inverse Phi Phi transpose, explain its dimensions, and distinguish this evidence covariance from the weight posterior covariance.

lessons.title: Select hyperparameters with evidence, not training fit
lessons.deck: Balance fit and normalisation without confusing selection and evaluation.

prerequisites.title: Before this lesson
prerequisites.detail: Read the Gaussian log-density as a fit term plus a normalisation term. Validation chooses settings on held-out data; evidence uses the training dataset’s marginal density.

lessons.teachback: Explain why optimising evidence can use the training data without a separate tuning split, and why that does not remove the need to assess generalisation.

lessons.title: Read the regularisation and evidence demonstrations
lessons.deck: Interpret the source’s fits, validation curves and evidence comparison.

prerequisites.title: Before this lesson
prerequisites.detail: Recall lambda = sigma² alpha for the stated PLS convention. Training, validation and test errors answer different questions.

lessons.teachback: Walk through slides 14–17: identify underfit and overfit, what validation selects, what evidence selects, and what the reported test numbers do and do not establish.

lessons.title: Occam’s razor is an average, not a maximum
lessons.deck: Understand complexity through prior-weighted likelihood averaging.

prerequisites.title: Before this lesson
prerequisites.detail: Recall evidence = integral of likelihood times prior. A normalised density has finite total mass even when its support covers a large space.

lessons.teachback: Use the dataset-space schematic to explain why a flexible model can fit very well yet have lower evidence. Why does the weight prior matter?

lessons.title: Learn regularisation and observation noise together
lessons.deck: Read joint evidence maps and distinguish noise variance from standard deviation.

prerequisites.title: Before this lesson
prerequisites.detail: Distinguish sigma from sigma²; know why taking logarithms makes positive hyperparameters easier to display and why evidence includes a determinant.

lessons.teachback: Explain the raw and log evidence heat maps and the zoomed noise estimate. How does lambda relate to prior precision and noise variance, and why is naive training-error tuning inadequate?

lessons.title: Derive the Type-II predictive mean and variance
lessons.deck: Derive the Gaussian prediction and its two variance contributions.

prerequisites.title: Before this lesson
prerequisites.detail: Know the Gaussian weight posterior and the law of total variance. Treat the new observation noise as independent of training noise and weights.

lessons.teachback: Derive the conditional predictive Gaussian and separate latent-function uncertainty from observation noise. Which uncertainty does Type-II still omit?

lessons.title: Read predictive bands where data are present and absent
lessons.deck: Interpret pointwise uncertainty bands and their modelling limits.

prerequisites.title: Before this lesson
prerequisites.detail: Use the predictive variance decomposition. A one-standard-deviation band is built from square roots of variances, not by adding standard deviations.

lessons.teachback: Interpret both predictive plots. Why does uncertainty grow in an unobserved region, and why is a narrow band not a guarantee that the model is right?

lessons.title: Beyond weights: basis families and RBF widths
lessons.deck: Preview integrating or selecting basis families and RBF widths.

prerequisites.title: Before this lesson
prerequisites.detail: Recall that every predictive distribution is conditional on modelling choices. Distinguish a discrete choice of basis family from a continuous width parameter.

lessons.teachback: Explain how basis choice and RBF width could be selected or averaged. What must be integrated to obtain evidence conditional only on those remaining choices?

lessons.title: Evidence and the implicit Occam effect
lessons.deck: Read the recap plots without confusing evidence optimisation with full marginalisation.

prerequisites.title: Prior predictive density
prerequisites.detail: Evidence averages the data likelihood over a normalised parameter prior; it is a density for continuous targets.

prerequisites.title: Precision and regularisation
prerequisites.detail: The weight prior has precision alpha; with fixed noise variance the ridge coefficient is lambda = sigma-squared times alpha.

lessons.teachback: Explain why a very flexible model can have lower evidence than a moderately flexible one, even when it achieves lower training error.

lessons.title: The full predictive target and the analytic roadblock

prerequisites.title: Marginalisation
prerequisites.detail: Integrating a joint density over an unknown variable removes it while preserving its uncertainty in remaining variables.

prerequisites.title: Conditional prediction
prerequisites.detail: Given weights and noise scale, a new target is Gaussian around the fitted function; the new input is fixed.

lessons.teachback: Write the full predictive integral and explain why an analytically Gaussian weight posterior does not make all hyperparameter integrals analytic.

lessons.title: Type-II estimation: what it keeps and what it discards

prerequisites.title: Gaussian covariance

prerequisites.title: Density and change of variable

lessons.title: What the RBF width changes

prerequisites.title: Basis functions

lessons.teachback: Explain what changes when r changes, how that differs from changing alpha, and why integrating alpha and sigma does not yet integrate r.

lessons.title: Bounded log priors and consistent integration measures
lessons.deck: Translate the source priors into normalised densities before integrating.

prerequisites.title: Substitution in an integral
prerequisites.detail: If sigma changes to v = sigma-squared, the integration element and density must both change.

prerequisites.title: Proper prior
prerequisites.detail: A proper density integrates to one; finite positive log-scale bounds provide a normalisation constant.

lessons.title: Numerical evidence: grid quadrature is not iid Monte Carlo

prerequisites.title: Expectation

prerequisites.title: Conditional predictive

prerequisites.title: Bayes on grid cells
prerequisites.detail: Posterior cell mass is proportional to likelihood times prior cell mass, followed by normalisation.

lessons.teachback: Derive posterior grid weights and the mixture mean and variance. Which uncertainties are retained, and why is r still a plug-in approximation?

lessons.title: Integrate width and compare basis families

prerequisites.title: Mixture weights

prerequisites.title: Model evidence

sourceWarnings.text: The source PDF clips the right-hand indirect-dependence column. Missing text is not reconstructed; consult the visible original and treat this preview as incomplete.
Timetables, assessment arrangements and historical course details are transcribed source material, not current administrative guidance.
Historical legal/medical examples and the dated applications on slide 24 are lecture case studies, not independently updated facts or professional guidance.
Full predictive derivations, evidence-based fitting of alpha/noise variance and model/basis-width selection are signposted for later lectures, not taught in full here.

A p-value is a tail probability under a specified null model, not the posterior probability that deaths were accidental or that a hypothesis is true. Treat the quoted case-study interpretation critically, alongside the dependence and selection discussion.
The printed joint-probability annotation involving 1 in 1,500 is unclear. No reliable replacement estimate is inferred; the lesson explains the dependence principle instead.

The 250-fold comparison uses event occurrences per example rather than a pair of labelled-event marginal probabilities. The lesson preserves the slide arithmetic and explains this denominator ambiguity.

The claim that every department favours female applicants is not literally supported by the supplied counts: Medicine is 99/416 versus 140/578, both rounded to 24%. The lesson uses the exact rates and explains the weighted-mixture effect.
MAP is Bayesian-derived, but a point estimate alone does not propagate posterior uncertainty; interpret the source’s slogan accordingly.
The analytic-roadblock claim depends on model and hyperprior choices; special conjugate cases can admit more exact integration.

Flat log-priors imply scale-coordinate Jacobian factors. Evidence maximisation is a log-coordinate posterior mode, not generally the mode of p(alpha, sigma² | y) in positive-scale coordinates. Improper priors need care for normalised evidence.
The Occam effect has no extra preferred log-alpha hyperprior here, but still depends on the weight prior. The source’s “not due to the prior” should not be read as prior independence.
The PLS degeneracy warning concerns naive training-criterion tuning, not impossibility of all non-Bayesian joint hyperparameter estimation.
The marked 0.212 and true value 0.250 are standard deviations, despite the vertical axis showing log variance. Slides 22–24 consistently label the horizontal axis log lambda.
The small PDF variance annotation has missing/clipped glyphs; transcription explicitly restores sigma_*² = sigma_hat² + phi_*^T Sigma phi_* from the Gaussian model and labelled contributions.
Flat priors in log coordinates are inverse-scale densities in raw coordinates. Evidence maximisation is not generally raw-coordinate MAP under those priors; density modes depend on coordinates.

The source switches between sigma and sigma-squared measures and calls a deterministic regular log grid Monte Carlo. Transform densities and bounds consistently; distinguish quadrature from iid random sampling.

The printed predictive sum suppresses training-data conditioning and omits normalisation. Use posterior cell masses proportional to likelihood times prior cell mass; equal prior-grid weights do not imply equal predictive weights. Width remains a plug-in estimate here.

The source prints three integral signs beside four differentials and gives a demo agenda rather than its outputs. No unseen demo results or winning basis family are reconstructed; family comparison requires proper priors and explicit model prior probabilities.

The source error integral is written over one target draw although the estimator depends on an entire sample. The 1/R result is variance for IID finite-variance draws; standard error is 1/sqrt(R). Dimension can affect the variance constant and sampling cost.
The continuation on PDF page 5 has blank problem-number references. Their connection to the preceding numbered list is inferred, not restored source text.

The CDF formula mixes theta and x as arguments, calls the CDF a cumulative density function, and reuses theta for the transformed output. Consistent notation and inverse-CDF endpoint limitations are explained alongside the transcription.
The absence of a closed-form hyperparameter posterior is the lecture example’s setting, not a universal theorem for all hyperpriors.
The source calls a regular-grid calculation Monte Carlo and refers to 1/R error. Grid quadrature is not IID Monte Carlo; 1/R concerns estimator variance.
The plotted target, integrand and proposal parameters are not supplied. Figures are preserved, but no exact curve definitions or simulated demo outputs are invented.
Non-converging Estimate is the source title. A finite plotted trace does not prove asymptotic inconsistency; the source lacks formulas needed to establish its tail moments.
The source switches target notation to P. Its high-dimensional impracticality conclusion is a generic warning about proposal mismatch, not a theorem ruling out all specialised importance methods.

The dimension-labelled figures span PDF pages 20–26. Their higher-dimensional regions are not explicitly defined; rounded percentages match nested Gaussian hypercubes at coordinate cutoffs 1.5 and 2.5, not fixed-radius spheres. The reconstruction and separate radial/shell derivations are labelled tutor support.

MCMC is a preview only. Local proposals alone are not a complete algorithm, and correlated chain draws need stationarity/ergodicity and suitable mixing conditions rather than the earlier IID assumption.
